topics.title: How your house is wired
topics.dek: Breakers, watts and the outlet with the two buttons

slides.h: Power arrives at the panel
slides.p: Utility lines feed a meter and then the breaker panel. In North America the service is 240 volts split into two 120-volt legs; most homes have 100 to 200 amps of capacity. Every circuit in the house starts at one breaker in that box.

slides.h: A breaker is a switch that trips itself
slides.p: Each breaker guards one circuit. When the current climbs past its rating it snaps off before the wire in the wall can overheat. To reset one, push it firmly all the way to OFF, then back to ON.

slides.h: Volts push, amps flow, watts work
slides.p: Watts are volts times amps. A 1,500-watt space heater on a 120-volt circuit pulls 12.5 amps, most of a 15-amp breaker by itself. That one line of arithmetic explains most tripped breakers.

slides.h: Why the same breaker keeps tripping
slides.p: Usually too much on one circuit: the heater and the hair dryer share a wall. Spread the big draws across rooms. A breaker that trips with nothing plugged in points to a short or a worn breaker, which is an electrician's job.

slides.h: GFCI: the outlet with the buttons
slides.p: A ground-fault circuit interrupter compares the current going out with the current coming back. A difference of about 5 milliamps, electricity leaking through water or through you, cuts the power in a fraction of a second. Codes require them near water: kitchens, baths, garages, outdoors.

items: Once a month, press TEST: the power should cut off
Press RESET: the power comes back
If it won't reset, the outlet has failed; replace it

slides.h: AFCI: the breaker that listens for sparks
slides.p: An arc-fault breaker recognises the electrical signature of arcing, the sparking of a frayed cord or a loose connection that starts many house fires, and trips. Newer codes require them for bedrooms and living areas.

a: Button on the outlet or breaker

slides.h: Extension cords are temporary
slides.p: Cords are rated by wire gauge; a thin 16-gauge cord can't safely feed a heater. Never run a cord under a rug or plug one power strip into another. A strip is only a surge protector if it says so and prints a joule rating.

items: Heavy 12- or 14-gauge cord for big loads
Cords under rugs or through doorways
A power strip plugged into a power strip
Surge protector: look for the joule rating

slides.h: When to call an electrician
slides.p: Warm outlets or switch plates, a burning smell, lights that dim when an appliance starts, buzzing from the panel, or aluminum branch wiring from the late 1960s and 70s. Anything inside the panel is not a weekend project.

quiz.q: A 1,500-watt heater on a 120-volt circuit draws about how much current?
quiz.why: Watts divided by volts is amps: 1,500 ÷ 120 = 12.5 amps, most of a 15-amp circuit on its own.

quiz.q: A GFCI outlet is there to protect you from…
a: Shock from current leaking to ground
quiz.why: It trips when the current going out and coming back differ by about 5 milliamps, which means some is leaking through water or a person.

quiz.q: A breaker trips with nothing plugged into the circuit. The right move is to…
a: Tape it in the ON position
quiz.why: A bigger breaker lets the wire overheat. A breaker that trips on an empty circuit is reporting a fault.

take: Watts = volts × amps; one space heater can fill a 15-amp circuit.
Test GFCI outlets monthly: TEST, then RESET.
Warm plates, burning smells and buzzing are calls to an electrician, not projects.

topics.title: Laundry, decoded
topics.dek: The care symbols, the temperatures and why towels go stiff

slides.h: The tag is a set of five symbols
slides.p: Every care label uses the same grammar: a tub for washing, a triangle for bleach, a square for drying, an iron for ironing and a circle for dry cleaning. Dots mean temperature, lines under a symbol mean a gentler cycle, and an X means don't.

slides.h: Dots are degrees
slides.p: One dot on the wash tub means cold (about 30 °C / 86 °F), two is warm (40 °C / 104 °F), three is hot (50 °C / 122 °F) and so on up to six. A hand in the tub means hand wash. The same dots on the iron mean low, medium and high heat.

slides.h: Cold water does most of the work
slides.p: Modern detergents are built for cold water, which keeps dyes in, slows shrinking and uses far less energy; heating the water is most of a wash cycle's electricity. Save hot water for sheets, towels and anything a sick person has used.

slides.h: Sort by colour, then by weight
slides.p: Whites, lights and darks, because dye migrates, and heavy items (jeans, towels) apart from light ones (shirts, delicates), because heavy things need longer to dry and beat up thin fabric. Zip zippers, empty pockets, turn prints inside out.

slides.h: Less detergent than you think
slides.p: The cap's lines are set for full, heavily soiled loads. Too much leaves residue that stiffens towels, traps odour and makes high-efficiency machines rinse extra. Start with half a cap; add more only if things come out dull.

v.c: what a 'full cap' is designed for

slides.h: Stains: act fast, start cold
slides.p: Blot, don't rub. Cold water first for protein stains (blood, egg, sweat): hot water cooks them in. Dish soap lifts grease; an oxygen bleach soak lifts coffee, wine and grass. Check that the stain is gone before the dryer sets it for good.

slides.h: The dryer is where clothes die
slides.p: Heat and tumbling shrink fibres and the lint trap is proof of wear. Dry on low or medium, pull things out slightly damp, and hang knits flat. Clean the lint screen every load: a clogged one lengthens drying and is a fire risk.

slides.h: Why towels go stiff, and the fix
slides.p: Fabric softener and detergent build up a waxy film that also makes towels less absorbent. Skip softener on towels, use less detergent, and once a month run them hot with a cup of white vinegar in the rinse, or a scoop of oxygen bleach.

items: Wash hot with no detergent and 1 cup of white vinegar
Wash again hot with ½ cup of baking soda
Dry on medium; shake out before folding

quiz.q: Two dots inside the wash tub symbol mean…
quiz.why: Dots are temperature: one is cold, two warm, three hot. Lines under the tub mean a gentler cycle.

quiz.q: A fresh blood stain should first be rinsed in…
quiz.why: Protein stains set with heat. Cold water first, then an enzyme detergent.

quiz.q: Towels have gone stiff and stopped absorbing. The likeliest cause is…
quiz.why: Softener and excess detergent coat the fibres. A hot wash with vinegar, then baking soda, strips the film.

take: Tub, triangle, square, iron, circle: dots are heat, lines are gentleness, X is don't.
Cold water, half a cap of detergent, low heat in the dryer.
Cold first for protein stains; hot water cooks them in.
src: U.S. Department of Energy: laundry energy use

topics.title: Inside the refrigerator
topics.dek: How it makes cold, where things should go and what the numbers mean

slides.h: A fridge doesn't make cold, it moves heat
slides.p: A refrigerant circulates in a loop. The compressor squeezes it into a hot gas, the coils on the back shed that heat to the room, the liquid expands through a valve and turns bitterly cold inside the box, where it soaks up heat from your food, and the loop repeats.

slides.h: Two numbers to remember
slides.p: Keep the fridge at or below 40 °F (4 °C) and the freezer at 0 °F (−18 °C). Most bacteria multiply fastest between 40 and 140 °F. The dial often isn't a temperature at all; a $5 fridge thermometer tells you the truth.

slides.h: The door is the warmest shelf
slides.p: It swings into the kitchen several times a day. Condiments, juice and butter live there happily; milk and eggs don't. The back of the bottom shelf is the coldest place and the right home for raw meat, on a plate, where it can't drip.

slides.h: The crisper drawers have a dial for a reason
slides.p: High humidity (vent closed) keeps leafy greens and herbs from wilting. Low humidity (vent open) lets ethylene gas escape from apples, pears and stone fruit, which would otherwise ripen and rot their neighbours.

slides.h: Some things don't belong in there
slides.p: Cold ruins tomatoes and turns potato starch to sugar. Onions, garlic and winter squash want a cool, dry, dark cupboard. Bread goes stale faster in the fridge than on the counter; freeze it instead. Honey never spoils and only crystallises when chilled.

slides.h: Leftovers: two hours, four days
slides.p: Food that has sat out for more than two hours (one hour above 90 °F) is a gamble. Cooled and covered, most cooked leftovers keep three to four days; freeze what you won't eat by then. Shallow containers cool faster than one deep pot.

slides.h: First in, first out
slides.p: Restaurant kitchens label and rotate so the oldest food gets used first. At home: new groceries go behind the old, leftovers get a date on the lid, and one shelf is the 'eat me soon' shelf you check before deciding what's for dinner.

slides.h: Keep it full, keep it clean
slides.p: A fuller fridge holds its temperature better when the door opens; fill gaps with jugs of water. Dust the coils once or twice a year, keep the door seal clean, and give it a few inches of breathing room so the heat it sheds can get away.

items: A fridge thermometer, checked now and then
A dollar bill held firm by the door seal
Hot pots straight in: let them cool first

quiz.q: The refrigerator should run at or below…
quiz.why: 40 °F is the top of the safe range; the freezer should be at 0 °F. Above 40 °F bacteria multiply quickly.

quiz.q: Raw chicken belongs…
a: On the bottom shelf, on a plate
quiz.why: The bottom back is the coldest spot, and nothing is underneath to drip onto.

quiz.q: Cooked leftovers, cooled and covered, are good for about…
quiz.why: Three to four days is the usual guidance; freeze anything you won't eat by then.

take: 40 °F fridge, 0 °F freezer; buy a thermometer.
Door warmest, bottom back coldest: raw meat low, milk in the middle.
Two hours out, then four days in.
src: FDA: Are you storing food safely?

topics.title: Home emergencies: the first five minutes
topics.dek: Where the shutoffs are, what the smells mean, and when to just leave

slides.h: Find three valves before you need them
slides.p: The main water shutoff (usually where the pipe enters the house, near the meter or the water heater), the gas meter valve outside, and the main breaker at the top of the electrical panel. Walk the house once and show everyone who lives there.

slides.h: A burst pipe: water off, then power
slides.p: Close the main valve (clockwise, or a quarter turn so the lever is across the pipe). Open the lowest faucet to drain the line. If water is near outlets or the panel, cut the breakers, but don't stand in water to do it. Then call a plumber and start photographing for insurance.

items: Open a low faucet to drain the pipes
Breakers off if water is near wiring

slides.h: A gas smell: leave, then call
slides.p: Natural gas is given its rotten-egg smell on purpose. If it's strong, don't flip switches, light anything or use a phone inside; open a door on the way out, get everyone away from the building and call the gas company or 911 from outside. Faint and localised near the stove? Check the burners are off and open windows.

items: No switches, lighters or phones inside
Call the gas company or 911 from outside
Don't go back until they say so

slides.h: Smoke alarms: one per level, test monthly
slides.p: Put them in every bedroom, outside sleeping areas and on every floor including the basement. Test monthly, change batteries yearly (or buy 10-year sealed units) and replace the whole alarm after ten years; the sensor wears out. Most fire deaths happen in homes with no working alarm.

v.c: then replace the whole alarm, not just the battery

slides.h: Carbon monoxide: the alarm you can't smell
slides.p: CO comes from anything that burns: furnaces, water heaters, gas stoves, generators, cars in a garage. It causes headache, nausea and drowsiness before it kills. Install CO alarms near bedrooms, and never run a generator or grill indoors or in the garage, even with the door open.

slides.h: A kitchen fire: lid, not water
slides.p: Grease fires explode when water hits them. Turn off the heat, slide a lid or baking sheet over the pan and leave it. An oven fire: close the door and turn it off. If flames reach the cabinets or you hesitate, get out and call 911; a pan isn't worth it.

a: Lid or sheet over the pan
Baking soda on a small flame
Leave the lid on to cool

slides.h: Power out: fridge closed, generator outside
slides.p: A closed fridge keeps food safe about four hours, a full freezer about 48. Unplug electronics so the surge when power returns doesn't fry them. Generators run outside only, 20 feet from windows. Check whether the whole street is dark before calling the utility.

slides.h: A kit by the door
slides.p: A flashlight that isn't your phone, a battery bank, a first-aid kit, a wrench that fits the gas valve, water (a gallon per person per day for three days), copies of IDs and insurance, and the phone numbers for the utilities written down, because the app needs a signal.

items: Wrench for the gas valve, by the meter
Insurance and utility numbers on paper

quiz.q: You smell a strong gas odour in the kitchen. First move?
a: Open windows and turn on the exhaust fan
Get everyone outside, then call from there
quiz.why: Any switch or spark can ignite it. Leave with the door open, then call the gas company or 911 from outside.

quiz.q: A pan of oil catches fire on the stove. You should…
a: Turn off the heat and cover it with a lid
quiz.why: Water makes burning oil erupt. Smother it, kill the heat and leave the lid on until it's cool.

quiz.q: A smoke alarm should be replaced entirely after about…
quiz.why: The sensor degrades. Batteries yearly, the whole unit at ten years; the date of manufacture is printed on the back.

take: Know the water main, the gas valve and the main breaker before anything happens.
Gas smell: out first, call second. Grease fire: lid, never water.
Smoke alarms on every level; CO alarms near bedrooms; replace alarms at ten years.

topics.title: The chemistry under the sink
topics.dek: What soap actually does, what disinfecting means, and what never to mix

slides.h: Soap works by grabbing both sides
slides.p: A soap molecule has a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail. The tails bury themselves in grease, the heads face the water, and the grease is lifted off in tiny bundles (micelles) that rinse away. That is why water alone can't clean a greasy pan and soap can.

slides.h: Clean, sanitize, disinfect: three different jobs
slides.p: Cleaning removes dirt and most germs with soap and water. Sanitizing lowers germs to a safe level. Disinfecting kills nearly all of them, and only works on a surface that has already been cleaned. For most of the house, cleaning is enough.

items: Clean: soap and water lift dirt and most germs
Sanitize: cut germs to a safe level (food surfaces)
Disinfect: kill nearly all of them (sick room, raw meat spill)

slides.h: Disinfectants need time to work
slides.p: The label's 'contact time' is how long the surface must stay visibly wet: often four to ten minutes. A quick spray-and-wipe is cleaning, not disinfecting. Read the small print, let it sit, then wipe or let it dry.

slides.h: Never mix these
slides.p: Bleach plus ammonia (in many glass cleaners) makes chloramine gas. Bleach plus vinegar or other acids releases chlorine gas. Bleach plus rubbing alcohol makes chloroform. Hydrogen peroxide plus vinegar makes peracetic acid. Use one product, rinse, then the other, with the window open.

slides.h: Acids for minerals, bases for grease
slides.p: Limescale, soap scum and rust are mineral deposits: vinegar, citric acid or a bathroom cleaner (acids) dissolve them. Grease and grime are organic: baking soda, degreasers and oven cleaners (bases) break them down. Match the cleaner to the mess and you scrub less.

slides.h: Vinegar is not a disinfectant
slides.p: It's a decent cleaner and a great descaler, but it doesn't reliably kill the germs that matter, and it etches marble, granite and grout and can cloud some finishes. Don't put it on natural stone, waxed wood or the rubber seals of appliances.

items: Kettle, shower head, coffee maker descaling
As a disinfectant for raw-chicken counters

slides.h: Microfibre beats paper
slides.p: Microfibre cloths are split fibres with far more surface area, so they lift dust and grease with water alone and trap it instead of pushing it around. Wash them without fabric softener, which clogs the fibres, and keep colours for kitchen, bath and floors.

slides.h: A simple order for any room
slides.p: Top to bottom so dust falls onto surfaces you haven't done yet, dry before wet so you aren't making mud, and left to right so you don't miss a patch. Finish with the floor.

items: Disinfect the touch points: handles, switches, taps

quiz.q: Mixing bleach with an ammonia-based glass cleaner produces…
quiz.why: Chloramine gas irritates the lungs and can be dangerous in a closed bathroom. One product at a time, rinse between.

quiz.q: To actually disinfect a counter with a spray, you must…
a: Let it stay wet for the label's contact time
Use it on a dirty surface so it has something to kill
quiz.why: Disinfectants need minutes of wet contact, and work only on a surface that has already been cleaned.

quiz.q: Limescale on a tap is best dissolved with…
a: An acid such as vinegar or citric acid
A base such as baking soda
quiz.why: Scale is a mineral deposit; acids dissolve it. Bases are for grease.

take: Cleaning removes; disinfecting kills, and only on a clean surface, with time.
Bleach mixes with nothing: not ammonia, not vinegar, not alcohol.
Acids for scale, bases for grease; vinegar off the stone.
src: CDC: Cleaning and disinfecting your home

topics.title: How the heat and the AC work
topics.dek: The furnace, the heat pump, the filter and the thermostat

slides.h: A thermostat is just a switch with an opinion
slides.p: It compares the room to the setting and calls for heat or cooling. The system runs until the room overshoots by a degree or so, then rests. Programmable or smart thermostats save money by not heating an empty house, not by being clever about the furnace itself.

slides.h: A gas furnace in four parts
slides.p: Burners heat a metal heat exchanger; a blower pushes house air across it and through the ducts; exhaust leaves through a flue. Modern units are 90 to 98 percent efficient. The one part that must never crack is the exchanger, because that is what keeps the exhaust out of your air.

slides.h: Air conditioning is a refrigerator for the house
slides.p: Same loop as the fridge: refrigerant absorbs heat indoors at the evaporator coil, the compressor pumps it outside, the condenser coil dumps the heat to the yard, and the fan you hear is blowing it away. Water dripping from the unit is humidity pulled out of the air, which is why rooms feel drier.

slides.h: A heat pump is an AC that runs backwards
slides.p: Flip a valve and the same loop pulls heat from the outdoor air, even cold air, and delivers it inside. Because it moves heat rather than making it, it delivers two to four units of heat per unit of electricity. Cold-climate models now work well below freezing; a backup heat strip covers the coldest nights.

slides.h: The filter is the cheapest fix in the house
slides.p: It protects the blower and coil from dust. A clogged filter starves the system of air, makes it run longer, and can freeze the coil. Check it monthly; most need changing every one to three months. MERV 8 to 11 balances filtration and airflow for most homes.

slides.h: Where the money goes
slides.p: Heating and cooling are roughly half of a typical home's energy bill. The big levers are a tight envelope (attic insulation, sealing leaks), a sensible setback when you're out or asleep, and a system that is maintained, not a system that is new.

slides.h: Set it and leave it
slides.p: Turning the thermostat way up doesn't heat the house faster; the furnace has one speed. A setback of 7 to 10 degrees for eight hours a day can cut heating and cooling costs by up to about ten percent a year. Ceiling fans should push air down in summer and pull it up in winter.

v.c: saved by setting back 7–10 °F for 8 hours a day

slides.h: A once-a-year checklist
slides.p: Change the filter, hose the outdoor unit's fins (power off first), keep two feet clear around it, clear the condensate drain, vacuum the supply registers, and have a technician check the heat exchanger and refrigerant charge. Noises, short cycling and ice on the lines are calls to make now, not in July.

quiz.q: A heat pump heats a house by…
a: Moving heat from outdoor air indoors
quiz.why: It's an air conditioner run in reverse. Because it moves heat instead of making it, it delivers more heat energy than the electricity it uses.

quiz.q: The furnace filter should be checked…
quiz.why: Monthly checks, changes every one to three months. A clogged filter strains the blower and can freeze the coil.

quiz.q: Setting the thermostat to 85 °F will heat a cold room…
a: At exactly the same speed as 70 °F
quiz.why: A single-stage furnace is on or off. It will just keep going past 70 and waste energy.

take: Heating and cooling are about half the energy bill.
Filters monthly; MERV 8–11 for most homes.
A heat pump is an AC with a reversing valve, two to four times as efficient as resistance heat.
src: U.S. Department of Energy: Home heating systems
U.S. Department of Energy: Heat pump systems

topics.title: How the plumbing works
topics.dek: Traps, vents, the water heater and the toilet that won't stop running

slides.h: Two systems that never touch
slides.p: Supply lines bring pressurised clean water in (about 40 to 60 psi). Drain-waste-vent pipes carry used water out by gravity alone, which is why they slope and are much larger. Every fixture sits where the two meet.

b: gravity, sloped ¼ in per foot

slides.h: The P-trap is a water seal
slides.p: The U-bend under every sink holds a plug of water that blocks sewer gas from coming up the drain. A drain that smells after a vacation has usually just dried out; run the tap. The trap also catches rings and earrings, which is why it unscrews by hand.

items: Water flows down and around the U-bend
Some stays behind as a seal
Sewer gas can't get past the seal
Dry trap = smell; run water to refill

slides.h: Why there's a pipe sticking out of the roof
slides.p: Vents let air into the drain system so water can fall freely, like the second hole in a juice can. Without them, draining water would suck the traps dry. A gurgling sink or a slow drain everywhere at once often means a blocked vent, not a blocked pipe.

slides.h: A running toilet is almost always the flapper
slides.p: Lift the tank lid. The rubber flapper seals the hole to the bowl; when it wears, water trickles out and the fill valve keeps topping up. A new flapper costs a few dollars. If the water level is above the overflow tube, adjust the float instead.

items: Put food colouring in the tank; wait 15 minutes
Colour in the bowl? The flapper leaks
Water over the overflow tube? Lower the float
Hissing fill valve? Replace it (also cheap)

slides.h: The water heater: 120 degrees
slides.p: Set the thermostat to 120 °F (49 °C): hot enough for dishes and showers, cool enough to slow scalding and mineral build-up, and it saves energy. Drain a few gallons from the bottom valve once a year to flush sediment. Tank heaters last about ten to fifteen years.

slides.h: Chemical drain cleaners are a last resort
slides.p: They can damage old pipes, and if they don't clear the clog you're left with a sink full of caustic liquid. Try a plunger with the overflow hole covered, then a drain snake. Grease belongs in the trash, not the drain; it cools and sets like candle wax in the pipe.

items: Hand snake or a zip strip for hair
Boiling water for soap and grease (not PVC-only)
Grease, wipes, 'flushable' anything down the drain

slides.h: Every fixture has its own shutoff
slides.p: Under sinks and behind toilets are small valves. Turn them off before any repair and once a year just to keep them from seizing. If a valve won't close or drips when turned, close the main and replace it: a stuck valve is the one you'll need at 2 a.m.

slides.h: Frozen pipes and water hammer
slides.p: Pipes on outside walls freeze first; in a hard freeze, let a thread of water run and open the cabinet doors. If a pipe freezes, open the faucet and warm it slowly from the faucet back; never with a flame. Banging when a tap closes is water hammer: an arrestor or draining the system to refill the air chambers quiets it.

quiz.q: The water held in the P-trap under a sink is there to…
quiz.why: The plug of water is a seal. When a trap dries out the room smells; running the tap refills it.

quiz.q: A toilet that runs on and off all day most likely needs…
quiz.why: A worn flapper lets water trickle into the bowl and the fill valve keeps topping up. The dye test confirms it.

quiz.q: The recommended water heater setting is…
quiz.why: 120 °F limits scalding, slows scale build-up and saves energy; most tanks ship set higher.

take: Supply is pressure; drains are gravity and need vents to breathe.
Smell at the drain: refill the trap. Running toilet: flapper first.
Water heater at 120 °F; flush sediment yearly; exercise the shutoffs.
src: U.S. Department of Energy: Water heating

topics.title: What goes in which bin
topics.dek: Recycling without wishful thinking, and a compost pile that doesn't stink

slides.h: Rules are local, but the big ones travel
slides.p: Programs differ by city, so check yours. Nearly everywhere takes clean paper and cardboard, metal cans, glass bottles and jars, and plastic bottles and jugs. Nearly nowhere wants plastic bags, food-soiled paper, or anything smaller than a credit card.

slides.h: The number inside the triangle isn't a promise
slides.p: The resin code (1 to 7) says what kind of plastic it is, not that your program recycles it. Bottles and jugs stamped 1 (PET) and 2 (HDPE) have real markets. Tubs marked 5 (PP) sometimes do. Films, foam (6) and mixed 'other' (7) mostly don't.

slides.h: Empty, clean, dry
slides.p: A little residue is fine; a half-full yogurt cup contaminates the paper around it. Rinse, shake out, and leave caps on bottles (they're captured in the process now). Don't bag recyclables: bags jam the sorting machinery and workers pull them out by hand.

items: Quick rinse, no need to scrub
Loose in the bin, never bagged

slides.h: Wish-cycling makes things worse
slides.p: Tossing a doubtful item in 'just in case' sends it down a line built for something else. Plastic bags wrap around sorting drums; batteries start fires in trucks and facilities. When in doubt, throw it out, and take bags back to the grocery store bin.

slides.h: Compost is browns plus greens
slides.p: Carbon-rich 'browns' (dry leaves, cardboard, paper, straw) and nitrogen-rich 'greens' (fruit and vegetable scraps, coffee grounds, grass clippings), roughly two to three parts brown to one green by volume. Too many greens and it smells; too many browns and nothing happens.

slides.h: What stays out of a backyard pile
slides.p: Meat, fish, dairy and oily food draw animals and go rancid. Pet waste and diseased plants carry pathogens. Glossy paper and 'compostable' plastics need an industrial facility's heat. Eggshells, tea bags without staples and paper towels are fine.

items: Fruit & veg scraps, coffee grounds, eggshells

slides.h: Air and water are the other ingredients
slides.p: The microbes doing the work need the pile as damp as a wrung-out sponge and turned every week or two to let oxygen in. A hot, working pile reaches 130 to 160 °F in the middle and finishes in a few months; a lazy pile just takes a year.

slides.h: Reduce still beats recycle
slides.p: Recycling saves energy (an aluminum can from recycled metal takes about 95 percent less than from ore), but about a third of what goes in a bin is contaminated or unrecyclable. The bigger win is less packaging in the first place: refills, bulk, and the bag you already own.

v.c: less energy to make a can from recycled aluminum than from ore

quiz.q: Plastic grocery bags should go…
a: Back to the store's drop-off bin or the trash
quiz.why: Bags and film jam the sorting machines. Grocery stores collect them separately.

quiz.q: A healthy backyard compost pile is mostly…
quiz.why: Roughly two to three parts browns to one part greens. Too many greens and it turns slimy and smells.

quiz.q: The number in the recycling triangle on a plastic container tells you…
a: What kind of plastic it is
How many times it's been recycled
quiz.why: It's a resin code. Whether your program accepts it is a separate question; bottles and jugs (1 and 2) usually, films and foam rarely.

take: Empty, clean, dry, loose: never bagged.
The triangle number is a material, not a promise; 1 and 2 bottles and jugs are the sure things.
Compost: two parts brown to one green, damp as a sponge, turned for air; no meat or dairy.
src: EPA: How do I recycle common recyclables?
